claims.text: Introducing a sacrificial oxide former such as cerium into high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles can overcome structural or chemical instability during catalytic operation.
The starting nanoparticles are crystalline, near-equiatomic, single-phase solid solutions containing at least five metals.
Cerium can function as a sacrificial oxide former when introduced into the alloy nanoparticles.
The intervention is intended to operate throughout 773–1173 K.
Introducing the sacrificial oxide former will produce a stable oxide layer.
The sacrificial oxide former reacts with oxygen to form the proposed stable oxide layer.
The stable oxide layer protects the underlying alloy from further oxidation.
The stable oxide layer protects the underlying alloy from structural or chemical degradation.
Nanoparticles containing the sacrificial oxide former will be more stable than otherwise identical nanoparticles without it.
Nanoparticles containing the sacrificial oxide former will exhibit better catalytic performance than otherwise identical nanoparticles without it.
The relevant boundary conditions include repeated or sustained exposure to both oxidative and reductive environments.
The exact mechanism and interaction of the sacrificial oxide former with the alloy nanoparticles are not fully understood.
In-situ XAFS can be used to assess structural stability during thermal exposure.
A lack of improved XAFS-indicated stability and catalytic activity relative to an untreated baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
